content: The Great Plague of Seville, which occurred between 1647 and 1652, was a catastrophic outbreak of disease in Spain that resulted in the deaths of approximately 60,000 people, amounting to nearly 25% of Seville's population. Unlike the earlier plague of 1596-1602, which primarily affected northern and central Spain as well as Andalucía, this outbreak is believed to have originated in Algeria and initially struck eastern Spain. The city of Valencia was the first to be affected, suffering an estimated loss of 30,000 lives. The disease then spread through Andalucía and moved northward into Catalonia and Aragon. Along the coast of Málaga, the death toll reached upwards of 50,000 individuals. The city, along with its surrounding rural areas, is estimated to have lost 150,000 people, which represented a quarter of its total population of 600,000. This level of devastation had a profound and lasting impact on Seville and the economy of Andalucía, from which they never fully recovered. Across Spain as a whole, the Great Plague is thought to have claimed the lives of 500,000 people, which was nearly 5% of the country’s total population of just under 10 million at the time. To put this into perspective, in a modern nation with a population of 300 million, this would equate to the loss of approximately 15 million individuals. This outbreak was the most severe but not the only plague to afflict Spain during the 17th century. Less than 25 years later, Spain faced another devastating epidemic. Between 1676 and 1685, a plague swept through the country in waves, causing widespread suffering. It was particularly severe in Andalucía and Valencia. The situation was exacerbated by a poor harvest in 1682-1683, which led to famine conditions and further weakened an already vulnerable population. This final plague of the 17th century, combined with the famine that followed, is estimated to have caused an additional 250,000 deaths. In total, three major plagues ravaged Spain during the 17th century: 1. The Plague of 1596-1602 2. The Plague of 1647-1652 3. The Plague of 1676-1685 When accounting for normal births, deaths, and immigration, historians estimate that the cumulative death toll from these plagues throughout the century was at least 1.25 million people. As a result, Spain’s population remained stagnant between 1596 and 1696, showing little to no growth over the course of the century. The disease responsible for these outbreaks is widely believed to have been the bubonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. This bacterium is typically transmitted to humans via fleas that infest rats, which act as the primary vector. Other forms of the disease, such as septicemic plague and pneumonic plague, were also present during these outbreaks, contributing to the high mortality rates.
